newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: PM may turn to right to build new Slovenia govt.
newsitem.headline: PM may turn to right to build new Slovenia govt.

text.p: Slovenia's centre-left Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek said on Friday he would seek to build a new coalition government and hinted he may approach his main political rival, the conservative People's Party.
Liberal Democrat leader Drnovsek won a parliamentary vote on Thursday, supporting his mandate to form Slovenia's third government since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.
"I will try very seriously to enlarge the coalition and form a broader government," Drnovsek told a news conference.
"According to the election result, it would be most appropriate to reach a coalition agreement with the People's Party," he added.
Drnovsek, who has to present his government line-up before parliament within 15 days, said talks with other parliamentary parties would begin next week.

Drnovsek won the parliamentary vote with the slimmest of margins by 46 votes to 44 with backing from former communists and other small parties. A Christian Democrat deputy tipped the balance in Drnovsek's favour after defecting from his party.
A right-wing alliance consisting of the People's Party, centre-right Social Democrats and Christian Democrats opposed Drnovsek's bid for a second term in office.
The Liberal Democrats won 25 of 90 parliamentary seats in the November 10 general election, followed by the People's Party with 19.
A new Drnovsek government got the thumbs-up from the Ljubljana bourse and most economic analysts welcomed the result of the parliamentary vote as a positive sign for the markets.
Slovenian shares continued their bull-run on Friday with the SBI index closing 1.47 percent higher at 1,290.5. Traders said Drnovsek's nomination as premier would encourage buying.

Danilo Grasic, head of the investment sector at Slovenia's branch of Creditanstalt bank, said Drnovsek should not have too big a problem preparing Slovenia for membership of the European Union and NATO.
The Ljubljana government signed an association agreement with the EU last year and Drnovsek said Slovenia should become the first former Yugoslav republic to join the EU by 2001.
"I think no party, not even the opposition, will be able to afford a non-European policy," Grasic said.

"Drnovsek's nomination represents continuity of economic policy and political stability. It is a positive sign for capital markets. I expect the number of foreign investors will slowly increase," he added.
But Drnovsek may have an uphill task to persuade one or more of the right-wing parties to join the coalition.
"At the moment it seems that the parties are blocked," Drago Zajc, a professor of politics at the Ljubljana University's Faculty of Social Sciences, told Reuters.
"Drnovsek may have to work with a minority government and look for broader support on certain issues," he said.
President Milan Kucan appealed to all parties to bury the hatchet and work towards fresh cooperation.
"The time of confrontation now has to be replaced by a time of cooperation in the interest of the state," Kucan told a news conference.
